abstract: Monocular hand mesh estimators commonly predict rig parameters and project the mesh to obtain 2D keypoints. We find that directly predicted 3D joints agree better with 2D predictions, and fitting a mesh to predicted points reduces mesh error. We present FAH (Fast and Accurate Hand Estimation), a family of models built on SAM 3D Body’s hand branch through fine-tuning and feature distillation. The models predict corresponding 2D and 3D joints and surface points, fit MANO or MHR-Hand, and optionally estimate anatomical parts and contact without object geometry at inference. Causal refinement reduces acceleration error, and camera estimation places the hands in world space. Experiments show improvements in image-space alignment, hand geometry, contact estimation and world-space tracking over the evaluated baselines. The default ViT-L model runs at 65 fps with mesh fitting on an RTX 4070 Ti SUPER, or 49 fps with parts and contact enabled. The smallest ViT-S model reaches 125 fps without mesh fitting, parts or contact. Code: https://github.com/noahcao/FAH.

sections.body:
Most mesh estimators regress MANO or MHR rig parameters and project the mesh to 2D, so articulation, shape and camera errors reach the 2D landmarks. In a controlled comparison within one network, directly predicted 3D points agree better with the 2D predictions, and fitting a mesh to them is more accurate than predicting MANO parameters (Sec. 4.4).

FAH replaces SAM 3D Body's decoder and rig head with a heatmap head for corresponding 2D and 3D joints and surface points. The introduction lists three contributions: point prediction followed by mesh fitting, contact and video and world-space estimation, and a family of models running at 27–101 fps with mesh fitting on an RTX 4070 Ti SUPER.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Rig-based hand estimators propagate articulation errors to 2D landmarks, so FAH predicts points and fits meshes separately.

sections.body:
Single-image methods regress MANO parameters from a hand crop. HaMeR trains a large ViT on mixed 2D and 3D data, WiLoR adds a detector and in-the-wild data, Hamba uses graph-guided Mamba blocks, and AnyHand adds synthetic data. SAM 3D Body jointly recovers body and hands with a promptable decoder and the MHR rig, and FAH builds on its hand branch.

For egocentric and world-space work, HaWoR combines a temporal model with DROID-SLAM and metric depth, and ViDiHand uses a video diffusion model. For contact, HACO estimates per-vertex contact from one image, while distance rules on reconstructed meshes require object shape and pose. FAH predicts contact from hand features and geometry.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior work regresses mesh parameters or vertices, and some contact methods need object shape and pose.

sections.body:
FAH starts from SAM 3D Body's hand branch, a DINOv3-H+ teacher with its promptable decoder and rig head removed. Feature distillation initializes DINOv3 ViT-S/16, ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16 students. The decoder-free pose network predicts 21 MANO-convention joints, two points inside each of the 20 bones, and 400 farthest-point samples of the 778 MANO vertices, each in crop-normalized 2D and root-relative 3D. The full surface is rebuilt from the 400 points using the lowest 200 eigenfunctions of the template's cotangent Laplacian.

A mesh stage fits MANO or MHR-Hand to these points. The detector is a one-stage YOLOv8m segmentation network at a 640 px input. Optional part and contact heads run on the frozen pose network.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: FAH distills SAM 3D Body's hand branch into ViT students and predicts dense 2D and 3D points with a heatmap head.

sections.body:
The experiments cover five settings: egocentric 3D on HOT3D v1 (98 five-second clips) and EgoStandard (120 thirty-second clips, aggregate metrics only), image-space pose on bench2d v2 (8.6k hands), contact on HOT3D and DexYCB s0 with HOI4D and ARCTIC, world-space tracking, and throughput on an RTX 4070 Ti SUPER.

In Table 1 on HOT3D v1, FAH-L (the default) reaches 65 fps with PA-MPJPE 4.31 mm and PA-MPVPE 4.02 mm, against 6.72 mm and 6.49 mm for WiLoR at 4.7 fps. Video rows add causal refinement. Reported contact and world-space results depend on the stated benchmark subsets and intervals.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: On the egocentric benchmark, the default FAH model's aligned joint error is 4.31 mm, below WiLoR's 6.72 mm.

sections.body:
The paper states three limitations. Camera estimation dominates world-space error, and better camera trajectories remain an important direction. Contact without object geometry is ambiguous: most contact vertices are hidden on 96% of HOT3D contact hands, and the head also fires on hand-face and hand-hand contact in in-the-wild videos, although training labels cover only hand-object contact.

FAH prioritizes real-time inference over maximum accuracy. Stronger segmentation or optical-flow models could improve supervision and camera estimates, but each change needs evaluation against extra computation. The conclusion states that FAH predicts corresponding 2D and 3D points, fits MANO or MHR-Hand, and runs in real time on a consumer GPU.
sections.heading: Limitations and Conclusion
sections.headline: Camera estimation dominates world-space error, and contact remains ambiguous without object geometry.

sections.body:
This appendix describes how the released models are trained. The teacher is SAM 3D Body's hand branch, fine-tuned for 10k steps on 384 px crops. Feature distillation trains DINOv3 ViT-S/16, ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16 students for 20k steps through a two-layer adapter. Pose training uses AdamW with weight decay 0.01, gradient clipping at 1.0, and degradation augmentation for low light and egocentric views.

Table 9 lists sources and sampling shares, such as HOT3D at 150k crops and COCO-WholeBody at 58k. Label conventions convert 3D sources to kinematic MANO joints. Image credits are listed in Appendix D.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists training sources, teacher and student settings, label conventions, and image credits.
